The “Rat Boy” reference comes from the season 6 episode of The Simpsons titled “Homer vs. Patty and Selma,” which first aired in 1995. In the scene that spawned the meme, Homer is hiding a financial crisis from Marge and tries to butter her up by calling her his “loyal wife” and Lisa his “little princess”. When he gets to Bart, however, he absentmindedly refers to him as “dear Rat Boy,” causing Bart to indignantly exclaim, “Rat boy? I resent that!”. Homer immediately follows this by telling Bart to “stop gnawing on the drywall,” further leaning into the rodent-like comparison. The image you provided shows Lisa standing in the hallway during this exchange, a still that is often used in memes to represent a sibling watching another sibling get “roasted” or mistreated by a parent.

This is one of the most powerful lines in *The Town* (2010), as it lays bare the film’s central conflict: the tension between loyalty to a lifelong way of life and the possibility of building something better. Directed by and starring Ben Affleck, the story follows Doug MacRay, a bank robber from Charlestown, Boston, who attempts to escape the fate that defined the lives of his family and friends. Yet, the closer he gets to starting a new life, the harder it becomes to leave behind the people who represent home to him. The film is about more than just spectacular heists; it explores how parental choices impact their children, the cycles that repeat generation after generation, and the price one must pay to break them. That is why this line hits so hard: sometimes we believe being a hero means making a sacrifice for everyone, when in reality, the hardest thing to do is simply be there for those who need us most.

Sirens (2014) is a comedy series that follows three Chicago paramedics who are incredibly skilled at saving lives but completely hopeless when it comes to managing their own. The show centers on Johnny, a veteran paramedic with commitment issues; his level-headed partner Hank; and Brian, their naive and overly enthusiastic new recruit. Together, they navigate bizarre emergency calls, workplace politics, and chaotic personal relationships, balancing the intense pressure of their jobs with plenty of workplace banter and offbeat humor.

I have no idea how to explain this movie to anyone: Swiss Army Man (2016)

*Swiss Army Man* is one of those movies that sounds impossible to sell until you understand what it’s actually trying to do.

Daniel Radcliffe plays Manny, a corpse stiffened by rigor mortis for most of the film, yet he somehow makes the character feel weird, lovable, and emotionally human.

The Daniels made their directorial debut with this movie after coming from the world of music videos—including *Turn Down for What*—and it shows. They blend absurd humor, awkwardness, and genuine sadness in a way that never loses the film’s heart.

🎬 2000s animation studios really had a specific agenda when it came to designing female characters…

It wasn’t just the art style.
It was the expressions, the attitude, the outfits, the way they moved, even the personality they were given.

A lot of studios were out here creating characters with bold femininity, confidence, heavy screen presence, and a visual style that basically imprinted itself on an entire generation.

And yeah—looking at it through today’s lens, a lot of those scenes would probably be handled differently.

The industry changed.
The humor changed.
The way characters are written and portrayed changed too.

But one thing is hard to argue with:

Those designs had *serious identity*.
They didn’t feel generic at all.

They had style, charisma, and that kind of energy people still randomly remember years later.

A pretty obvious truth:

2000s animation studios knew exactly what they were doing.

🎬 Life of Pi is a 2012 adventure drama film directed and produced by Ang Lee and written by David Magee. Based on Yann Martel’s 2001 novel, the film stars Suraj Sharma in his feature film debut, alongside Irrfan Khan, Tabu, Rafe Spall, Gérard Depardieu, and Adil Hussain. The story follows Pi Patel, a 16-year-old Indian boy, and a Bengal tiger named Richard Parker, who are stranded together on a lifeboat for 227 days after a shipwreck.

Development on the film began shortly after the novel was published. Before Ang Lee was hired, directors M. Night Shyamalan, Alfonso Cuarón, and Jean-Pierre Jeunet were attached to the project at different stages.

Filming took place across India, Taiwan, and Montreal in 2011, with Rhythm & Hues Studios (R&H) handling the visual effects.

*Life of Pi* had its world premiere as the opening film of the 50th New York Film Festival at the Walter Reade Theater and Alice Tully Hall in New York City on September 28, 2012. It was released in U.S. theaters on November 21, 2012, by 20th Century Fox.

The film was a commercial success, grossing over $609 million worldwide, making it Ang Lee’s highest-grossing film. It received widespread critical acclaim and earned numerous accolades, including three Golden Globe nominations for Best Motion Picture – Drama, Best Director, and Best Original Score, winning the latter.

At the 85th Academy Awards, *Life of Pi* received eleven nominations, including Best Picture and Best Adapted Screenplay, and won four Oscars, including Best Director for Ang Lee.
